source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα λέγει ὅτι. εἰ δέδοκτο αὐτῷ ταῦτα. καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πειθόμενος ἐκολάζετο, δῆλον ὅτι θεῷ γε ὄντι καὶ βουλομένῳ οὔτ᾿ ἀλγεινὰ οὔτ᾿ ἀνιαρὰ ἦν τὰ κατὰ γνώμην δρώμενα. καὶ οὐχ ἑώρακέ γε αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ παρὰ πόδας ἐναντία εἰπών. εἰ γὰρ ἔδωκεν ὅτι ἐκολάζετο. ἐπεὶ δέδοκτο αὐτῷ ταῦτα. καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πειθόμενος ἐμπαρεῖχεν ἑαυτὸν, δῆλον ὅτι ἐκολάζετο, καὶ οὐχ οἷόν τε ἦν μὴ εἶναι ἀλγεινὰ τὰ προσαγόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν κολαστῶν· ἀπροαίρετον γὰρ ὁ πόνος. εἰ δὲ βουλομένῳ οὔτε ἀλγεινὰ οὔτε ἀνιαρὰ ἦν τὰ προσαγόμενα, πῶς ἔδωκε τὸ ἐκολάζετο; οὐχ ἑώρακε δὲ ὅτι ἅπαξ ἀναλαβὼν τὸ διὰ γενέσεως σῶμα ἀνείληφεν αὐτὸ καὶ πόνων δεκτικὸν τυγχάνον καὶ τῶν τοῖς ἐν σώμασι συμβαινόντων ἀνιαρῶν, εἰ τοῦ ἀνιαροῦ μὴ ὡς προαιρετικοῦ ἀκούοιμεν. ὥσπερ οὖν βουληθεὶς ἀνείληφε σῶμα οὐ πάντῃ ἄλλης φύσεως παρὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην σάρκα. οὕτως συνανείληφε τῷ σώματι καὶ τὰ ἀλγεινὰ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ ἀνιαρὰ. ὧν πρὸς τὸ μὴ παθεῖν κύριος οὐκ ἦν, ἐπὶ τοῖς διατιθεῖσιν ὄντος προσάγειν αὐτῷ τὰ ἀνιαρὰ καὶ τὰ ἀλγεινά. προαπελογησάμεθα δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ὅτι βουληθεὶς μὴ ἥκειν εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων οὐκ ἐληλύθει ἄν. ἦλθε δὲ. ἐπεὶ ἐβούλετο. διὰ τὸ προαποδεδομένον ἐκ τοῦ αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποθανεῖν τῷ παντὶ χρήσιμον.
pass_a_gloss: After these he says that: 'if these things had been resolved (δοκέω, δέδοκτο) by him, and obeying (πείθομαι) the Father (πατήρ) he was punished (κολάζω), it is clear that to [one] being a god and willing (βούλομαι) the things done according to his judgment (κατὰ γνώμην) were neither painful (ἀλγεινά) nor grievous (ἀνιαρά).' And he did not see that he said contradictory things to himself on the spot (παρὰ πόδας). For if he granted (δίδωμι) that he was punished, since these things had been resolved by him and obeying the Father he gave himself up (ἐμπαρέχω ἑαυτόν), it is clear that he was punished, and it was not possible that the things applied (προσάγω) by the punishers (κολασταί) not be painful; for pain (πόνος) is not subject to choice (ἀπροαίρετον). But if to one willing the things applied were neither painful nor grievous, how did he grant 'he was punished'? He did not see that, once having taken up (ἀναλαμβάνω) the body through birth (γένεσις), he took it up as being receptive (δεκτικόν) of pains and of the grievous things befalling those in bodies, if we do not hear 'grievous' as [something] of choice (προαιρετικόν). As therefore willing he took up a body not wholly of another nature (φύσις) than human flesh (σάρξ), so he took up together (συναναλαμβάνω) with the body also its painful and grievous things, of which he was not master (κύριος) so as not to suffer, it being in the power of (ἐπί + dat.) those disposing/treating (διατίθημι) [him] to apply to him the grievous and painful things. We have defended beforehand (προαπολογέομαι) in the earlier [parts] that, willing not to come into hands of men, he would not have come; but he came, since he willed, on account of the [reason] given before (προαποδίδωμι), from his dying for men (ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων) [being] useful (χρήσιμον) to the whole (τὸ πᾶν).
pass_b_english: After this he says: “If he had resolved on these things and was punished in obedience to the Father, it is clear that, since he was a god and willed it, what was done to him in accordance with his own will was neither painful nor grievous.” He did not see that he was contradicting himself in the same breath. For if he granted that Jesus was punished, since he had resolved on these things and in obedience to the Father gave himself up, it is clear that he was punished, and it was not possible that what the punishers inflicted should not be painful; for pain does not depend on the will. But if, because he willed it, what was inflicted was neither painful nor grievous, how did he grant that “he was punished”?

He did not see that, once Jesus had taken up the body that comes through birth, he took it up as a body capable of pains and of the grievous things that befall those who are in bodies, provided we do not take “grievous” to mean something that depends on the will. So, just as he willingly took up a body not altogether different in nature from human flesh, so together with the body he also took up what is painful and grievous in it. It was not in his power not to suffer these things, since it lay with those who were dealing with him to inflict grievous and painful things upon him.

We have already answered above that if he had willed not to come into the hands of men, he would not have come. But he came, because he willed it, for the reason already given, that his dying for men would benefit the whole universe.

choices.why: κατὰ γνώμην: 'by his own decision' -> 'in accordance with his own will'
ἀνιαρά kept as 'grievous' throughout (it was 'griefs' in two places)

choices.term: not wholly of another nature than human flesh
choices.why: calque removed: 'not wholly of another nature than human flesh' -> 'not altogether different in nature from human flesh'

choices.term: ὧν πρὸς τὸ μὴ παθεῖν κύριος οὐκ ἦν
choices.why: ὧν πρὸς τὸ μὴ παθεῖν κύριος οὐκ ἦν: 'He was not master of these, so as not to suffer them' -> 'It was not in his power not to suffer these things'
τῷ παντί: 'the whole world' -> 'the whole universe'; translator note updated to match

translator_notes: Staged punctuation splits clauses with full stops (‘ὅτι. εἰ δέδοκτο αὐτῷ ταῦτα. καὶ’, ‘ἐκολάζετο. ἐπεὶ’, ‘σάρκα. οὕτως’, ‘ἀνιαρὰ. ὧν’, ‘ἄν. ἦλθε δὲ. ἐπεὶ ἐβούλετο. διὰ’); read continuously. θεῷ γε ὄντι in Celsus’s words rendered ‘since he was a god’ (house convention for Celsus); τῷ πατρὶ ‘the Father’ capitalised because it refers to God the Father. ἀπροαίρετον γὰρ ὁ πόνος: ‘pain does not depend on the will’ (it is not a matter of choice). εἰ τοῦ ἀνιαροῦ μὴ ὡς προαιρετικοῦ ἀκούοιμεν: Origen separates bodily distress from the soul’s willed grief; rendered ‘provided we do not take “grievous” to mean something that depends on the will’. κύριος here means ‘master’ (in control), not the divine title; rendered ‘it was not in his power’. τῷ παντὶ rendered ‘the whole universe’. ‘We have already answered above’ points back to Origen’s earlier replies in Book 2 (around 2.9–2.10 and 2.16–2.17); exact place not certain. Possible echoes not cited inline: ‘come into the hands of men’ (compare Matthew 17:22; Mark 9:31) and dying ‘for men’ (compare John 11:50); both are too general to count as clear allusions here.
